raw_comment:
I notice that Japan lives longer than any other country in the world. I wonder why India has the lowest life expectancy and the lowest health spending of all countries shown on the graph.     
This is how it's going to impact my community. Healthcare is more scarce in my community because I am latino, and the graph demonstrates that paying more in the United States does not guarantee obtaining more. I'm curious if the pharmaceutical business and increased drug prices play a role in this. I have family members who require medication to treat illnesses, and the cost of the medication has risen over time despite no actual or minor improvements to the medication. For many families, the choice is between getting life-saving prescriptions and eating food that night. This shorter comparative life expectancy is most likely due to higher drug pricing. And this will probably be my headline “How is your life worth.”

raw_comment:
I noticed that India spends alot less money on health expenditure unlike the US, and just as expected the life expectancy for India is around 70 while the US is 76; not much of a difference in my eyes. I wonder, what would happen to the citizens of the other countries if their leaders decided to spend alot more money on healthcare just like the US. Would they end up just as bad as the US or be even better? The impact that this has on my community is that, the US spends a high amount of money on health expenditures and yet the life expectancy is alot more less than those countries that spend very little. raw_comment: first finding in this graph was that Japan leads the world in life expectancy, despite spending less on healthcare than several other major European countries and the United States. India spends amongst the least on health expenditures and also has the lowest life expectancy. The US, however, spends the greatest amount yet has a lower life expectancy than many other nations. These observations led to several questions on the state of health expenditures worldwide. First, do the health expenditures reflect how much consumers are spending on healthcare or an individual government? Furthermore, could the lifestyle and choices of individual citizens affect average life expectancy regardless of how much a country spends on healthcare? And lastly, how do countries such as China, Italy, and Japan maintain a higher life expectancy despite spending far less on health expenditures? The statistics of this graph lead to a deeper story with many important lessons that affect our country. As an American, it is important that our government is utilizing its health expenditures and funding in a way that best benefits the public. Unfortunately, despite spending nearly $10,000 per capita on healthcare, the results on life expectancy have largely plateaued. By studying countries such as Japan and Switzerland, we can learn methods that can increase life expectancy and better influence our decisions. I would title this graph: “The Price of Life.”

raw_comment:
I notice that The U.S. has the highest health expenditures per capita by far. That said, it isn't even that close to having the highest life expectancy. Germany, Switzerland, Italy, Japan, Canada, and France all spend less on health care and have higher life expectancies. I wonder how strong the correlation is between health care expenditures and average life expectancy. It is clear that in general countries that spend less on health care per capita tend to have lower life expectancies, with the exception of Saudi Arabia (which spends about as much as Italy). That said, countries with the highest life expectancies cover a large range of health expenditures per capita (Italy and Switzerland have similar life expectancies but differ in expenditures). This makes me wonder what other factors are at play. The impact that health care spending in the U.S. has on my community and everyone who lives in the U.S. is monumental. The leading cause of bankruptcies in the U.S. is medical issues, which cause around 530,000 families to file for bankruptcy each year. Universal health care is also relevant in U.S. politics, something that every country on this graph with the highest life expectancies has.

Headline: Healthcare Spending Not the Only Factor in Life Expectancies, as Shown by Exorbitant U.S. Healthcare Prices

raw_comment:
One of the most noticeable things about the graph is that those in the US spend the most on healthcare but have a sub-par life expectancy compared to other countries. This calls into question what the money we pay for healthcare is really going towards. Are health conditions in other countries just better? Does the US healthcare system essentially scam their citizens for profit? In my community, healthcare availability is more sparse and the graph shows that paying more in the US doesn't mean getting more. I wonder if Big Pharma and inflated prices of important medications play in this. I have family with type II diabetes and the cost of insulin has been rising over the years despite no actual or few improvements to the drug. And for many families, the decision comes to get the lifesaving medications or to have dinner that night. This inflated pricing of medications most likely plays a part in this lower comparative life expectancy. 
Title Idea: US Healthcare: All the Buck for No Bang

raw_comment:
I notice that the US spends significantly more on healthcare than all other countries; the US outspends the country that spends the second most on healthcare by approximately $2,000 per capita. Yet, the US has a lower life expectancy than countries that spend up to $8,000 per capita less. That leads me to wonder how big of a role pharmaceutical subsidies and inflated medical prices play in the overall healthcare expenditures. I live in a very rural community thus the impact of health expenditures and life expectancy has a larger impact on my community. Rural communities don't have access to the caliber of healthcare service that can be accessed in urban areas. This graph demonstrates that even increasing expenditures won't necessarily improve life expectancy. This will have an acute impact in rural areas, as cooperations could use data like this to justify not expanding, and even cutting back, services in rural areas. 
Catchy title: Better Healthcare, Better Costs? Think Again...

raw_comment:
I notice that countries with high qualities of life, such as Japan, Switzerland, and Canada, have much higher life expectancy rates compared to the US. The good qualities of life and the fact that these countries invest in healthcare for their citizens definitely contributes to the high life expectancy.
I wonder why the US does not invest more in funding for our healthcare system to help our elderly population live longer. The is evidence that shows that people won't suddenly begin to live longer, but is something that must be maintained through the whole life. Taking good care of yourself, and being able to afford to see a doctor, when nessecary, would greatly help improve the gap of the United States and the rest of the countries shown.
This negatively impacts me and my generation, because we have the facts to conclude that we will not live as, long as many of the people in my age group in other countries around the world. 
A catchy title for the graph would be, "Is having a high quality of life related to a country having high life expectancy rate?"

I also noticed that the top three countries were Japan, Switzerland, and Italy. The only one out of these three countries I did not expect to see, was Italy. Now, if that has any relation to the graph, I am unsure of it, but longevity and healthcare are definitely relevant so I deemed it to be relevant.

I wonder why the price ranges are shown on the x-axis. Could it possibly be how much an average person spends on medical fees weekly? monthly? yearly? 

The impact this graph has on me and my community is a question. I am wondering why are we not higher up even though we are seen to spend the largest amount of money on longevity?

I think a catchy headline for this graph would be 
"Is it worth it in the long run?"

raw_comment:
Doing The Most Or Doing The Least Is Not Necessarily Doing The Best
-By Justin Wright
“Doing The Most Or Doing The Least Is Not Necessarily Doing The Best”. That’s the title of this comment right? So let’s dive into what that means. The two variables being explored in this data are life expectancy at birth and health expenditure per capita. Now when we analyze the 13 countries on this graph, there seems to be no correlation between these variables. The United States spends over two times as much as Japan, yet Japan still has a higher life expectancy. China on the other hand spends almost a tenth of what the United States spends and still has a comparable life expectancy. I wonder why that is. I also observe that the 6 countries with higher life expectancies than the US, all have universal healthcare. It seems that socialized medicine, which has become quite the buzzword in American politics, is doing quite alright for itself. I wonder the impact this graph could have on American communities, knowing that the money the US is spending is not improving their life expectancies in comparison to other countries. And if the money spent is not improving their life expectancies, where is it going? Or maybe the better question is, to whom?

raw_comment: When I looked over the graph, I noticed that the countries that spent over $4,000 per capita look a lot different on the graph than the countries that spent below $2,000 per capita. First off, the <2,000 countries only spent an average of $11.20 per capita per each year of life expectancy. You could say that means the populations of the <2,000 countries spend an average $11.20 spent for each year of life expectancy. What about the >4,000 countries? Well, they average a lofty $75.50 per capita per each year of life expectancy, which is nearly seven times what the >2,000 countries spend. That is quite a difference. There must be a reason, possibly benefit for spending this much more. Well, there is. The <2,000 countries average a life expectancy of ~73 years while the heavy-spending >4,000 countries average a life expectancy of ~82 years. So their benefit for spending six times as more is nine extra years of life expectancy. Is it worth it? I’m not sure, because there are so many other variables.

raw_comment: When I first looked at this graph, I was heavily confused. How could a country like the United States spend so much on their health but still not have a top 5 life expectancy? I had the inverse reaction to China’s place on this graph, since communist leader Xi Jinping has been linked to many disappearances such as the disappearance of billionaire Jack Ma, and also has given the green light on the mass genocide of Uighur Muslims in so called “Re-Education” camps. China seems like a place where the life expectancy would be low, due to a communist government and terrible air quality, but it’s actually about 7 years ahead of India, which is also known for terrible air quality. So how do they do it? According to Wikipedia, 95% of the nation’s people have healthcare, so 5% of people isn’t enough to bring the average spending down to less than 1,000 dollars.  So really, why? That question will be unknown, but as China begins its rise as a global power, maybe that question will be answered.

raw_comment: The whole time I was looking at this graph I was thinking about, ‘How do we (The United States) spend the most amount of money on this graph and not even have close to the highest life expectancy rate’. Before for looking at this graph I would have assumed that the country that spends the most on health care would have the highest life expectancy rate, but there is no correlation. This really makes me wonder how the U.S. can spend so much money yet still have a really low life expectancy rate, but no matter how this happens it really effects our community. One effect that this has on our community is that people are sometimes less inclined to seek out medical help for seemingly small problems because it costs so much and it seems like the problem isn’t that bad, but then it can turn into a bigger problem that gets worse and worse. Then the problem becomes harder to treat because the person waited so long to seek out medical help.

We spend nearly 10,000 in Health Expenditure yet still fail to reach the upper echelon of countries. The only thing we can definitely say about this graph, is that there is no correlation at all. Money really can’t give you life. So what does?

raw_comment: Money=Life? 10,00 dollars. That’s how much we as citizens of America spend on our health’s. The graph is a perfect example of zero correlation. Health Expenditure per capital has very little influence over how long we live. You’d think the more we spend, the more years we can buy. That’s not even the worst part, draw your gaze to America. We spend nearly 10,000 in Health Expenditure yet still fail to reach the upper echelon of countries. Money really can’t give you life. So what does? There has to be some underlying factor that creates this sort of imbalance. There is a place called Roseto, Pennsylvania. The people there were studied during the 20th century. The people there lived longer, and had less case of heart attack than anybody else in America. The odd, part was that they smoked, drank, were fat, and ate terrible food regularly. The scientist there where nothing short of amazed. How could this place have such a long lifespan, yet be so unhealthy. The answer was community. The Rosetans, lived with 3generations under one roof. They worked hard to care for one another. We can look at the top country and find a similar correlation. Japan’s cultural background is similar. Their entire culture is based on honor, and kindness. What can we learn. That maybe our communities in America should turn from spending more money on health, and instead on following the Rosetans model of community. In turn maybe we can see a little more life, in a better country.

raw_comment:
Is the U.S. wasting its money on healthcare? According to a graph I analyzed, the United States spends the most money on healthcare. It showed the correlation between life expectancy at birth and healthcare expenditure per capita between thirteen countries. The United States spends roughly $3.3 billion a year on health care alone and our life expectancy is 79 years old on average.   To most, this might seem reasonable, but Japan's life expectancy on average is five years longer, and they only spend $630 million a year. That is five times less than what we spend annually. Like Japan, France, Canada, Italy, and Germany all spend between four to five thousand dollars per capita and have a life expectancy above 80. What are we doing wrong? 
	Japan requires all of its residents to join their healthcare system as a category called statutory insurance. This requires them to apply for healthcare on one of the 1447 plans available. It's paid for by tax revenue, allowing the average person to only spend $5,000 a year. In the U.S. the average person spends $10,000 a year on healthcare insurance. To receive healthcare benefits you must apply unlike in Japan where it is mandatory for everyone. The U.S. has roughly 37 million people who do not have healthcare insurance. Making people aware of the differences in each countries healthcare policy might make us change how we view healthcare.

raw_comment:
Life expectancy is not something a lot of people think about. The people who do think about it most, assume that if they live in a wealthy country then they will live longer than those who do not. After examining a graph, about average life expectancies and the amount spent on medical care I was very surprised. The graph shows how much a country on average would spend on medical care and how long their average life expectancies are. I saw that the two variables have zero correlation. For example, the United States citizens are spending the most on medical care but on average are living less long than those who live in Japan, Italy, France, Switzerland, Germany, and Canada.
	 I think that some of the reasons other countries have a longer life expectancy than the United States are because of the environment of those countries. According to U.S.News, the best countries by the quality of life and social purpose in rank are Canada, Japan, Germany, Switzerland, Australia, United States, New Zealand, United Kingdom, Sweden, and the Netherlands. This makes me wonder if the lurking variable is quality of life and social purpose. It also makes me think that in the United States we have less of a positive quality of life than those countries. In the United States, everyone is always competing against each other to best at your job or to be the most popular. I think that in the countries that put less importance on making money and being popular the citizens are happier and live longer.

raw_comment: Your country might be killing you! The graph has given us a intriguing and positive correlation between health expenditure and what the life expectancy is of that country. After further observation I realized that there is almost 0 correlation between these two variables. For example Japan spend much less than the U.S. on healthcare but has significantly longer life expectancy. Although those two are outliers the others follow the trend. Another example is India who almost spends no money on healthcare and has a very low life expectancy. I wonder if there is another lurking variable and why Japan has a much higher life expectancy, yet spend much less then other countries. Another interesting thing is that the U.S. spends so much on healthcare but has a average life span. It made me think that all the money might not be going to healthcare and maybe other things. The impact this could have is people might want to move to countries with higher life expectancy instead of the amount spent on healthcare.

raw_comment: The graph shown is interesting and shows some surprising stats. It is common knowledge that Japan is a very advanced country and has the highest life expectancy, but the reason for why Japan was the highest was unknown. The line that shows Japan's stats is ironic, since it has a considerably lower health expenditure per capita than the US, but has higher life expectancy. I assume this is because of the land size and the population. The land size could affect it because since Japan has a smaller land area than the US and does not need to spend as much money for shipping and traveling costs. Also, the population of Japan is lower and the US's population is 3 times higher which means it needs to spend more money on health. I also wonder why Switzerland is as high as Japan. Yes, it spends more money, but what is making its life expectancy higher that the United States isn't able to replicate. Another thing I wonder is why China has a low health expenditure per capita but has a population of over 1 billion. This could be because of its communist party. The impact this has on my community, since I live in the US, is how my family and my health care is being prevented or limited. I personally have not been affected, but I wonder why the curve is going down for life expectancy. My opinion is that it could be those greedy insurance companies. Also, this doesn't affect my community in much extent since some of my relatives are over 90. Headline: "Health expenditure vs Life expectancy"

raw_comment: On graphs of worldwide healthcare, there is a significant positive correlation between how much countries spend on healthcare per capita and life expectancy. This ranges from nations like India and Russia who do not spend much on healthcare and have low life expectancies, along with nations like Japan and Germany, that spend more on healthcare per capita and have very high life expectancies. The United States is an outlier on this graph. Americans, on average, spend more on healthcare than any nation. Switzerland, the second highest spending, spends about $2,000 less than the United States. However their life expectancy is about 79 years, which is in the middle, closer to nations like Saudi Arabia and China, as opposed to other western developed nations like Canada. People in the United States spend more than any other county and in return get an average life expectancy.

raw_comment: Want to live a long healthy life? Spend money on health expenditure! Is this really true? According to a graph created by World Bank, there might be a slight positive correlation with longer life expectancy and money spent on health expenditure. However this does not apply to all of the information. Japan, with the longest overall life expectancy is nowhere near spending as much as the United States, Germany, or Switzerland. These countries spend thousands of more dollars on health expenditure and yet, their life expectancy is many years lower than Japan. After researching the exact definition of “Health expenditure”, I found that this does not include the cost of sanitation and water quality. I wonder if this lurking variable might contribute to Japan’s life expectancy, since it is surrounded by water. This graph may convince some countries to spend more money on health expenditure, when it may not make a difference to their life expectancy.

raw_comment:
Spend Less, Live Longer! A Guide to Higher Life Expectancy

Everyone expects that the less you spend the shorter your life will be because you can’t afford the health necessities in life, but what if that wasn’t true at all? In this graph it is comparing health expenditures per capita for multiple countries and life expectancy at birth for those countries. Some things that I noticed was how Italy and Japan spend less than half of what the US spends on health and they have a much higher life expectancy. I also noticed how the US spends the most on medical care and yet their life expectancy is mediocre. And their are some outliers like India where they spend close to nothing and die early, and Switzerland who spends a little bit less than the United States and still has a high life expectancy. But most countries spend around 3,000 to 6,000 and have higher life expectancies. What I wonder is how? How do countries spend almost half as much as the average American and live 2-6 years longer? I suspect it has to do with what people spend on health and if they are using that money spent wisely. Or others lifestyles maybe they don’t spend as much money on health, but they do lead a healthier life style with diet, exercise, and less stress. This graph is very surprising and could have important effects on the community. Like what people decide to spend their money on, or where immigrants decide to go, or even how much money the government funds towards healthcare.

raw_comment: Do you want to know how to live longer? Take a look at this graph and observe what’s happening. There are two variables, the amount the countries healthcare spending is and the average life expectancy. There isint really a distinct correlation between the countries but I guess you could say there is some sort of a “positive” correlation. You can see Japan has the highest life expectancy but only 4500 is being spent while the US spends the most at 10000 and has one of the lower life expectancy. raw_comment:
I noticed that the US has the highest health expenditure per capita (although it doesn't have the highest life expectancy). Japan has the highest life expectancy but a mid-ranged health expenditure. Saudi Arabia also has a high health expenditure for its respective life expectancy. I wonder what each country's healthcare covers. I also wonder what has a larger impact on life expectancy: lifestyle or medical aid/healthcare. The overall shape of the graph is a curve that starts drastically increasing and eventually plateauing. In general, countries with a higher life expectancy have a higher health expenditure. 

This impacts me and my community because the expense of healthcare is a huge topic in the US. Additionally, transitioning to a healthier lifestyle is being heavily pushed. Seeing that health expenditure is the greatest in the US but only life expectancy is not the highest, I'm curious as to what other countries focus on that allow for such a high life expectancy at lower costs. 

A headline could be, "Does Healthcare Need to be Expensive for Living a Longer Life?"

raw_comment:
1) I wonder why there is such a large economic gap between the U.S and other countries?
2) I noticed that even though the U.S spends the most money they do not have the greatest life expectancy. Japan has the highest life expectancy and they pay about $6,000 less.
3) Could it be that U.S citizens have more health problems and that's why the U.S spends so much money?

Health overall has a big impact on our community. I think one reason we spend so much money on health resources is because we don't promote enough appropriate and achievable health goals. I think as a society we expect people to be at their peak level of fitness in order to be considered healthy, and that obviously is not a reality for many people. Therefore many people don't make an attempt at leading a semi healthier lifestyle which can lead to expensive health problems and death.

I think a title that would fit this graph is: "How Much Money Are We Spending to Keep Ourselves Alive?"

I notice a relationship between life expectancy and health expenditures. The higher the health expenditures, the higher the life expectancy, though the United States is seen as an outlier. The U.S has a life expectancy of ~78 years old, yet it has the highest health expenditures, being at 10,000 dollars. Other countries like Japan and Italy have a much higher life expectancy; however, they have noticeably fewer health expenditures.
I wonder why the U.S has a lower life expectancy, while they have the highest health expenditures. Another question that comes to mind is why Japan holds the highest life expectancy. 
A possible headline that summarizes this graph is "Does paying more for health care result in a longer life?"

raw_comment:
In looking at this graph, I notice that since the year 2000, the life expectancy in many countries has increased. I also notice that the countries who spend the most money on healthcare have higher life expectancy numbers than most countries but not all. I wonder why the United States spends the most money on health expenditures yet their life expectancy is not the highest out of the countries. I also wonder why countries like Italy and Japan who spend $3-4k compared to the US at $10k have a higher life expectancy and what is it they are doing differently than us. This impacts my community because I live in the US and clearly we are using more money than majority of the countries yet our life expectancy is not as high as other countries. While living until 70-78 years old is old, the life expectancy in Japan is 84. 
New Headline: "What Are Countries Doing to Have a Higher Life Expectancy Rate?"

"How much would you pay for a higher life expectancy?"

raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed from this graph was that the United States was a different color, it is drifting away from the other countries, and Switzerland is the second fastest on the graph.

I wonder why the US is a different color from the rest and also despite being underneath Switzerland, is the farthest away from the rest. 

This does not really impact my community; however, it does tell me that compared to places such as Japan, Italy, France, and most notably Switzerland, my country has a lower life expectancy at birth. 

A catchy headline for this graph can be: "Countries Rising To The Top!"

## 1. Chart type
- **Multi-series line chart** (country trajectories over time on an x–y plot)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **multiple overlaid lines** in a single panel.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **direct labeling** of selected country lines.
- Uses **color emphasis**: one highlighted series (United States) and many muted background series.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Health expenditure per capita | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Life expectancy at birth | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Year (2000–2017) | Temporal | Order/progression along each line trajectory |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Separate line series; direct text labels for selected countries; color emphasis/de-emphasis |
raw_comment:
I noticed that the graph depicts many different countries with lines that show the life expectancy in each country. The graph also shows the health expenditure per capita. Some show an increase as life expectancy goes up health expenditure goes up as well. However, most countries on the graph have less than a thousand dollars spent on expenditures even when the life expectancy goes up. Lastly, I noticed how the US' health expenditures are the most, yet the life expectancy is lower than some countries. 
I wonder what the US can do to lower the health expenditures while maintaining or increasing life expectancy. I also wonder how Japan only spends have of the amount than the  US but has the highest life expectancy.
This impacts my community because living the US we are sometimes blind to how other countries heath care systems work. This graph puts in perspective what we are doing compared to other counties and how we should reflect on how to lower the cost
A headline for this graph could be "Does A Long Life Cost More Money?"

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who posted comments and replies.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of these graphs:  “Money Can’t Buy Health” by Princess of Tennessee, "Does Paying More for Healthcare Result in a Longer Life?" by Sukhpreet of Valley Stream North in New York, "How Much Does a Long Life Cost?" by Diane of USA, “Are the Wealthiest the Healthiest?” by Paul of Memphis and “The Cost of Living” by Owen, Kate, Gabe and Halimo of Eden Prairie, Minnesota.

You can continue to post.  Please check back by Friday, April 16 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex). 

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who thinks the U.S. could do much better at increasing life expectancy AND lowering health costs, and David Wilcox of Lawrenceville, New Jersey, who hopes that improvements in quality of life will accompany increases in life expectancy and decreases in health expenditures going forward.

raw_comment:
I notice that the more countries spend on their health care, the greater the life expectancy seems to be. India spends little on their health care and they have a comparatively low life expectancy. Comparatively, Switzerland spends quite a bit on their health care and has a relatively high life expectancy.

I wonder what's keeping the US where it is. Americans spend the most on their health care, yet we aren't anywhere near where the other richer countries are. Compared to France, Canada, Japan, Switzerland, Germany, and Italy.

Because of the expensive health care, Americans usually only go to the doctor's office/hospital if they really need to. Contrasting Canada, where it could take months to get even the most essential treatment.

A title for this graph is "Medically Inclined: The Cost of Growing Old." 'Medically Inclined' because of the graph's visuals, then 'The Cost of Growing Old' to combine both the Life Expectancy and Expenditure portions of the graph.

raw_comment:
The first thing that I notice is that the united states is the outlier in this graph. As the graph shows that the united states easily spends the most amount of money on health expenditures. I also notice that a few countries don't spend as much money on health expenditure as the united states yet they have a higher life expectancy at birth than the united states. I wonder why the countries that don't spend that much money have a higher life expectancy? I wonder if they use alternative and natural things that boost their life expectancy? I wonder how and why Switzerland has such a high life expectancy yet they use a very broad range of health expenditure per capita? The cost of health care is discussed all the time around me. It is never what type of health care it is but rather how much it costs. From the graph, it seems as though people who pay more live longer.

Title: "life expectancy compared to health expenditures"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that since 2000, the life expectancy in every country depicted in the graph has increased. However, the life expectancy of Americans has not increased as much as the life expectancies of citizens from other countries depicted in the graph. For example, even though the Russian Federation has a lower life expectancy than the United States, it increased from 66 to 72 while the life expectancy in the United States only increased from 77 to 78. I notice that the US has the greatest health expenditure per capita. Finally, I notice that Japan and Switzerland have the highest life expectancies. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why the life expectancy in countries such as India, Ukraine, and the Russian Federation have increased so much. I wonder why the health expenditures in the US have increased so much even though the life expectancy hasn't. 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
Health care is a huge topic of debate when discussing politics in my social groups. Most people believe that health care costs too much and prohibits the impoverished from having access to essential health care. The data in this graph supports this opinion.

How much are you paying for each additional (expected) year of life?

raw_comment:
“Life Expectancy vs. Health Expenditures” 

Our group noticed many things about this graph. For one, mostly European countries have the highest life expectancy. Another thing we noticed was that the lines for each country move around a lot but level out more at the top. We also saw that the countries are split into 2 relative groups, one with lower life expectancies and one with higher. The group with lower life expectancies mainly has countries in Eastern Europe or Asia. Lastly, we noticed that many countries spend less on healthcare compared to the US, yet still have higher life expectancies than us. Next, we thought about what the graph shows. We wonder why most European countries live longer than everyone else. We also wondered why the US has a lower life expectancy at birth, but a higher health expenditure per capita. Lastly, we wondered what factors contribute to Japan having the highest life expectancy at birth. Then we thought about what impact this has on our community. This impacts us and our community as the life expectancy is slightly lower than most countries for the United States and we are spending a lot of money on healthcare compared to other countries. The curve line for the U.S. was moving up and now it appears that it is going back down. Ultimately, the United States has some room for improvement when it comes to healthcare.

raw_comment: From this graph, our team noticed that it compares life expectancy to health expenditure rates from 2000-2017, Switzerland and the U.S. have the highest health expenditure per capita, also in many countries, life expectancy has plateaued. Lastly, based on the graph Japan has the highest life expectancy and India has the lowest. Some things we wondered: why does Japan have the highest life expectancy; How does the U.S. spend so much on healthcare and still roughly have the same life expectancy? The last thing we wondered was if life expectancy will continue to plateau or will it spike/drop again? For the impact, this topic is important to our community because it shows approximately how much we should be spending on our own health care before it levels off and becomes too much. This can also impact a set amount of money that healthcare is worth throughout every country to better help their people’s life expectancy. As healthcare continues to increase in price, the life expectancy seems to have leveled off and starts to stop increasing. Our catchy headline is “The Cost of Living”.

raw_comment: This graph shows the average life expectancy at birth and the average health expenditure per capita. Our group noticed that Japan tends to have the greatest life expectancy despite spending far less on health expenditures. On the contrary, we noticed that the United States spends an average of $10,000 per capita, but has an expected life expectancy of 78. We found that many Eastern and Asian countries spend far less on health than the West, yet have relatively high life expectancies. We wondered: Would the air quality in China affect an overall life expectancy? We also questioned, “What led to a large increase in China and Russia’s life expectancy, despite little increase in spending?” Additionally, we also inquired as to why the West spends far more on health expenditures but sees little gain in life expectancy compared to Eastern and Asian countries?” This graph and its data affect our community because our health care should contribute to a longer life expectancy. The more elderly people that are in my community, the more money will be spent on health care bills. Also, those in my community will average a life of 78 years. We would title this article, “The cost of life; does increased spending improve life expectancy?”

raw_comment:
Title: The Health Care Gap

We notice that Switzerland spends lots of money but also has a high life expectancy so they are getting their money's worth. China, Brazil, Ukraine, India, and the Russian Federation have very low high expectancy and low health care spending. The United States is the only country that doesn't seem to fit with the curve. It has high spending and a lower life expectancy than the other countries that spend the same amount. We wonder why the U.S. makes claims that they spend their money on health care for example and yet, it is bad for a lot of Americans? We wonder why the U.S. spends so much on health care expenditure, and yet Japan is living longer? Finally, we wonder what other factors perhaps help people live longer. What have Germany, Italy, Canada, and Japan done to have higher life expectancies when they don’t spend as much money on healthcare? This impacts our community because Americans pay the most for healthcare, but our life expectancy isn’t as high as countries that pay less than we do. For the most part higher spending on healthcare means that the life expectancy in that country will be higher than those that spend less. So what is America doing wrong that we spend the most and don’t have the highest life expectancy. We should be taking pointers from the countries with the highest life expectancy.

raw_comment: This graph shows how much various nations from around the world spend on healthcare, and how long citizens of those nations are expected to live. The first thing our group noticed was the highest paying nation was the United States, despite our life expectancy only being the 7th best on the graph. raw_comment:
I notice a relationship between life expectancy and health expenditures. The higher the health expenditures, the higher the life expectancy, though the United States is seen as an outlier. The U.S has a life expectancy of ~78 years old, yet it has the highest health expenditures, being at 10,000 dollars. Other countries like Japan and Italy have a much higher life expectancy; however, they have noticeably fewer health expenditures.

I wonder why the U.S has a lower life expectancy, while they have the highest health expenditures. Another question that comes to mind is why Japan holds the highest life expectancy. 

This impacts my community because even after having significantly higher health expenditures, our country doesn't have an exceedingly high life expectancy rate.

A possible headline that summarizes this graph is "Does paying more for health care result in a longer life?"

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows the relationship between life expectancy and health expenditures per capita (per person) since 2000 for countries around the world.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

Keep noticing and wondering.  There will be no graph next week.  The next graph on electric cars will be released by Friday, April 16 with moderation on Wednesday, April 28.

## 1. Chart type
- **Multi-series line chart** (country trajectories over time on an x–y plot)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **multiple overlaid lines** in a single panel.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- No stacking.
- Uses **direct labeling** of selected country lines.
- Uses **color emphasis**: one highlighted series (United States) and many muted background series.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Health expenditure per capita | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Life expectancy at birth | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Year (2000–2017) | Temporal | Order/progression along each line trajectory |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Separate line series; direct text labels for selected countries; color emphasis/de-emphasis |

This impacts us because our life expectancy is in the middle and we spend a lot of money on health compared to other countries.
4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
The graph shows life expectancy per country and health expenditures. A catchy headline would be "how long would you live>"

raw_comment:
I notice that this is a bivariable graph which compares life expectancy with health care expenditures in various countries. I notice that Japan and Switzerland seem to have the highest life expectancies. The U.S seems to have the highest health expenditures, however its life expectancy is lower than many nations. It seems like there is a positive correlation between life expectancy and health expenditures for these countries. However, this correlation is not entirely consistent (Saudi Arabia and the U.S are two outliers).
I wonder what health care expenditures are. Is this how much money a nation spends on its health care? I wonder which of these nations have free healthcare. Does free healthcare improve life expectancy? I wonder what other factors influence life expectancies other than health care expenditures.
This impacts my community because it seems like our nation spends a great deal of money on healthcare but we still have fairly low life expectancies. This leads me to believe that only a small few have access to our great healthcare. Many people in Memphis have no healthcare. If we distribute our well-funded healthcare more efficiently to the public by making it affordable, I’m sure our life expectacies could be that of Japan and Switzerland.

raw_comment: I notice that this is graphing the relationship between life expectancy and health expenditures across many countries. I see that generally the more life expenditures the higher the life expectancy. I see that the United States has a really high health expenditures but a lower life expectancy. Other countries like Switzerland have a lower health expenditure than the United States, but a higher life expectancy. I wonder as to why it is that we see the US having a lower life expectancy while it is one of the highest in health expenditure. Logically, you would think that the more money you spend on health, the higher your life expectancy but I can see that this does not follow true here. Many factors that we consider are although we do spend more on health expenditure, the United States is notorious for having very unhealthy foods and products. It only makes sense that we have lower life expectancies because of what we consume despite how much we spend on health. The impact that this has on me and my community is that it is setting us up for a lower life expectancy for US residents. I personally would like to live a long and healthy life, so I do my part in eating healthy and drinking plenty of water to do just that. Catchy headline: "Does Spending More Money on Health Increase Life Expectancy?"

raw_comment: I have noticed that the United States has low health care compared to other countries. Americans claim that the United States is the best country in the world, but when it comes to our citizen's well-being it's the lowest among other nations. Someone might expect that when it comes to health care expenditures there will be an increase. But, from 2000 to 2017, this relationship has not been consistent globally. I see that other states like Japan, France, and Germany have a higher life expectancy and what I have learned is that they make health care available for everyone. They don't even charge a single penny when going to the infirmary or clinic. I am guessing that the United States charges more for the hospital bill and that makes people want to spend less when it comes to getting their annual check-up. I wonder why the United States feels the need to charge more for individual health care? I wonder what the United States can learn from the other countries? I wonder how much money the government has to charge so much for many families? The question does on and on, but what I do know is that American health care is impacting a lot of families. Those who can't afford to go to the doctors and these families are in dire need of help. The graph is showing the relationship between life expectancy at birth with other countries. Seeing the graph makes me question America's intention so a catchy headline would be "The US Spends To Money on Health Care."

raw_comment:
What do you notice?I notice that some countries' expenditures match what I would assume the line of fit would be, but certain countries like the United States do not. I think for America this is because we have privatized healthcare that is more about money and politics and less about lives.
What do you wonder?
I wonder if  it is Japan's elevated  environment and healthy eating habits that has sustained them to live longer? 
What impact does this have on you and your community?
In the United States we see challenges with private healthcare due to pre-existing conditions.  People are not treated equally when it comes to healthcare.  I worry many people in my community will die unnecessary deaths due to the politics surrounding healthcare. How has the relationship between life expectancy and health expenditures by country changed since 2000?
Countries that have a higher life expectancy might also provide for their elderly population in different ways than other countries. There are many methods and cultural ways that each country uses per age population. In India there has been little growth throughout the years; while Switzerland, France, Italy and Japan have made strides and their people are beginning to live longer.  It is hard to determine if the price per expenditure is a factor because America spends a lot of money per person but has made little improvement on the rise in life expectancy.    Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
“The Price of Life.”

raw_comment:
What I notice:
- The US now spends the most in health expenditures but people aren’t living the longest
- India has the lowest life expectancy (around 69 years) in this graph but they also spend the least in health expenditures
- Japan doesn’t spend the most in health expenditures, but still has the highest life expectancy
- The US has generally the same life expectancy from 2000-2017 (76-78) though they’re spending more each year
- India has spent the least amount in health care, but their life expectancy has been improving (0-70)
What I wonder:
* What other factors are causing Japan to have the highest life expectancy because Japan doesn’t spend the most in health care?
* How come the US is spending more in health care but not improving in life expectancy? 
* If India spent more in health care, would it improve their life expectancy? 
* If the US spent less in health care, would it still maintain their life expectancy? 

In my community, we have about a 78 year old life expectancy and we spend the most (close to $10,000) in health expenditures. I think that we’re better than some countries but could improve.

A headline could be: How long are you expected to live?

raw_comment:
What I notice: 
1. I notice that the United States spends more money on health care, but it does not result in people living longer. 
2. I notice that India has the lowest health expenditure per capita and people don't live that long there.
3. People in Japan have the highest life expectancy, they spend more than India but less than the US on healthcare. 

What I wonder: 
1. I wonder why the US spends so much on health care expenditure but they don't have the highest life expectancy.
2. I wonder why Japan spends less, but the people live longer. 
3. I wonder what other factors help people to live longer. 

What impact does this have on you and your community:
 In the graph, my community has around a 78 life expectancy. I think that we are better off than some of the other countries.

Catchy Headline: 
How much money do you spend to live longer?

A catchy headline would be: will you live over 60 years?

raw_comment:
"TIME IS MONEY"

In the graph, I see many countries being compared about their life expectancy by health expenditure per capita. The health expenditure per capita means that country has a lot of capita and health expenditure. In the graph, India is outlined as the lowest and US as the highest in terms of health expenditure per capita. Switzerland is the best among all of the countries compared as it has more life expectancy
than united states and it is the second in health expenditure per capita.  Japan is outlined for the most life expectancy though.

I think what this graph's main message is that if the health
expenditure per capita (purchasing power parity) is higher, the higher the life expectancy at birth in the country. This is not constant for all countries, especially for United States.

I wonder why the lines are not consistent and why United States spends so much on health care expenditure but does not have a good ratio of life expectancy like the other countries. Another question I have is why does the health expenditure for some countries lower and still have a high life expectancy in the 
country.

This impacts my country because it makes us wonder what our country would rank in this graph and would it be worrying. This is because we would want to find out the issues that is causing out life expectancy to be the number it is and how our health expenditure affects it.

raw_comment:
‘Money Can’t Buy Health’

What do you notice? 

That the United States is at the threshold of proficiency but is going Predictably downward. Our health expenditures are the best though.   

What do you wonder? 

Since Americans are foreignly regarded as fat - and we are foodies - and since obesity is a big problem particularly in America, could this be affecting our life expectancy curves?

What impact does this have on you and your community? What's going on in this graph? 

To put it blatantly, this graph shows the money invested to ensure health (like health ensurance, etc.) in its relation to potentially achieving its intended worth (Ensuring you’re life expectancy with quality healthcare). If you’re an American you probably need to see this as we all - hopefully - generally pay for health coverage of some sort. (You don’t want to waste money on health if it doesn’t mean your life expectancy!) Our line (U.S.’s) on this graph is quite eye catching as with better Health funding longer life won’t have a better likelihood. Like this tells us that something Large scale is just a problem somewhere In America.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that some countries expenditures match what I would assume the line of fit would be, but certain countries like America do not. I would assume for America this is because we have privatized healthcare that is more about money and less about lives.
What do you wonder?
I wonder if Japan may want to lower their life expectancy as they are experiencing overpopulation(grim but a thought I had).
What impact does this have on you and your community?
As an American who has struggled with the concept of private healthcare due to my pre-existing condition I often worry in this country it has become far too political of an issue when it should have little to do with it.
What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
This graph showcases the relationship between spending and life expectancy so I would call it : "What to Expect, The Reality of Spending vs Life Length"

raw_comment:
I think that maybe the United States spends more money on healthcare per capita as it is a privatised, for-profit system. In almost all other countries, there is some form of Universal Healthcare and I suppose that healthcare is cheaper as a result. Governments are unlikely to try to squeeze profit out of citizens whereas, for the private sector, it is vital. 
Of the countries who have higher life expectancy (that are shown), all but Switzerland are in the G8, proving that more developed economies have an improved life expectancy as they are the only countries who can afford the greater health expenditure. Compared to the high income countries, the United States falls behind. Perhaps the world's biggest GDP does not automatically equal longer life.
Also, many of the lower expenditure countries have very quickly increased life expectancy judging by the steep gradient of the line, showing that they are developing at speed. The extra money spent at a lower level looks far more effective  at  increasing lifespan than when the country already spends a lot.
We can also see how Japan has a world-leading life-expectancy, maybe this is what is causing there old person crisis.
